title: Targeted Prep: Fractional Exponents + Downward Parabolas
subtitle: 8 Questions · ~30 min · Tuesday Warm-Up
purpose: Targeted Tuesday drill before Wednesday retake. Starts with two confidence questions (proven mastery areas) then drills the two skills RP12 will test harder: fractional exponents (Q3-Q6, escalating) and negative-a parabolas (Q7-Q8). Not a full exam : a focused primer.

questions.rationale: Confidence opener. Kai is 4/4 on radical equations. Same technique, new numbers. Gets him in the zone before harder material.
questions.hint: Isolate the √ first. Then square both sides.
questions.feedback_correct: Warm-up locked. Radical technique is solid.
questions.feedback_wrong: Subtract 3 first: √(6x+10)=10. Then square both sides.

questions.rationale: Second confidence opener. Kai is 4/4 on exponential same-base equations. Easy win before the targeted drill begins.
Simplest fractional exponent. One step: x^(2/3)=4, apply the reciprocal power 3/2. Answer is 8 : recognizable. Goal: build the mechanical pattern before adding a coefficient wrapper.
questions.question_html:
Solve: \( x^{2/3} = 4 \)
Hint: to undo x^(2/3), raise both sides to the 3/2 power (flip the fraction).
questions.hint: The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. Raise both sides to the 3/2 power. 4^(3/2) = (√4)³.
solution_steps: Raise both sides to 3/2 power: x = 4^(3/2).

questions.rationale: Adds a coefficient wrapper. Must isolate x^(2/3) first by dividing by 2. Then apply reciprocal power. Answer is 27 : recognizable (3^3). Same reciprocal power as Q3 but now with an extra step.
questions.hint: Divide by 2 first to isolate x^(2/3). Then apply the 3/2 power.

questions.rationale: Switches to 3/2 exponent (vs 2/3 in Q3-Q4). Reciprocal is now 2/3. Target: x^(3/2)=8 → x=4. Clean: ∛8=2, then 2²=4. Builds fluency with the other common fractional exponent.
questions.hint: Divide by 3 first. Then apply the 2/3 power (flip 3/2). ∛8 = 2.
questions.feedback_wrong: Divide by 3: x^(3/2)=8. Apply 2/3 power: ∛8=2, then 2²=4.

questions.rationale: Full RP-style wrapper: isolate, then apply 2/3 power. Answer x=9 via 27^(2/3). Most similar to the RP4 question Kai missed (2x^(3/2)-14=672). This is the confidence-clincher before the final exam.
questions.hint: Step 1: Subtract 20. Step 2: Divide by 4. Step 3: Apply 2/3 power. ∛27 = 3.
questions.feedback_wrong: Subtract 20, divide by 4: x^(3/2)=27. Apply 2/3: ∛27=3, then 3²=9.

questions.rationale: Introduces the negative leading coefficient. Kai has only graphed upward parabolas so far. This question asks him to identify that a<0 means opens DOWN and find both intercepts. Primes him for RP12-Q12.
questions.question_html: For \( f(x) = -(x - 1)^2 + 4 \): state the parent function, identify the vertex, state whether it opens UP or DOWN, and find the x-intercepts.
questions.hint: Vertex form: a(x-h)²+k. Vertex is (h,k). Negative a → opens DOWN. Set f(x)=0 to find x-intercepts.
solution_steps: The vertex (1,4) is a MAXIMUM since it opens down.
questions.feedback_correct: Negative a caught. Opens down. Both intercepts correct.
questions.feedback_wrong: a=−1 → opens DOWN. Vertex (1,4). Set f(x)=0: x=3 or x=−1.

questions.rationale: Full graph of a downward parabola with a stretch factor. Vertex (-1,8), opens DOWN, x-intercepts at 1 and -3. This is the hardest question in the drill and the most direct rehearsal for RP12-Q12.
questions.question_html: Graph \( f(x) = -2(x + 1)^2 + 8 \). State the vertex, direction, and x-intercepts.
questions.hint: a = −2 → opens DOWN, narrower than normal. Vertex is (−1, 8). Set f(x)=0 for intercepts.
solution_steps: Vertex form: −2(x+1)²+8 → vertex at (−1, 8). a = −2 → opens DOWN.
Draw inverted, narrower U from (−3,0) through vertex (−1,8) to (1,0).
questions.feedback_correct: Vertex, direction, intercepts, and graph all correct. Downward parabola locked.
questions.feedback_wrong: a=−2 → opens DOWN. Vertex (−1,8). Set f(x)=0: x=1 or x=−3.
